# R code chunks and regular text {#sec-chunks-and-text}

Anything that is not enclosed in the special chunk syntax, like this sentence,
is regular text. The two chunks below are R code.

**A chunk whose code and result both appear:**

```{r}
#| label: summary-cars
summary(cars)
```

**A chunk whose code is hidden, so only the plot appears:**

```{r}
#| label: plot-pressure
#| echo: false
plot(pressure)
```

The second chunk uses `echo: false`, which is why you see the figure but not the
code that drew it.

# Inline code {#sec-inline}

Values computed in R can be dropped into a sentence, so the numbers in your
writing update themselves when the data changes.

```{r}
#| label: inline-demo
set.seed(2334)
yield <- 200 * runif(100)
mean_yield <- mean(yield)
```

The average yield is `r round(mean_yield, 1)`, computed from
`r length(yield)` observations.

Look at the source of the sentence above: the numbers are written as inline R
code, not typed by hand.

# Markdown basics {#sec-markdown}

## A level-2 header

### A level-3 header

+ list item 1
  - a nested list item
+ list item 2
+ *italics*
+ **bold**
+ `code shown in a sentence`
+ inline math: what does $\int_a^b f(x)dx$ even mean?
+ a web link: [Markdown basics](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html)

Math on its own line:

$$\bar{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i/n$$

## Inserting a figure

A figure that lives in a file is inserted with this syntax:

````{verbatim}
![A caption for the figure](my_figure.png)
````

A figure produced by R is inserted by writing the code that draws it, and
labelling the chunk. See @sec-figure-options below.

## Citations

A citation is written `[@smith2020]`, where the key refers to an entry in a
`.bib` file named in the YAML header. Setting that up is covered in lecture
02-4, so it is only shown here, not used.

# Chunk labels {#sec-labels}

Every chunk in this file has a label, given with `#| label:`. The chunk below is
called `labelled-example`.

```{r}
#| label: labelled-example
n_rows <- nrow(cars)
n_rows
```

Labels make error messages readable, and they are required for the
cross-references you will meet in lecture 02-4.

# Chunk options {#sec-chunk-options}

## `echo` and `eval` {#sec-echo-eval}

**Both the code and the result (the default):**

```{r}
#| label: echo-eval-both
summary(cars)
```

**`echo: false`, so the code is hidden and only the result appears:**

```{r}
#| label: echo-eval-no-echo
#| echo: false
summary(cars)
```

**`eval: false`, so the code is shown but never run, and there is no result:**

```{r}
#| label: echo-eval-no-eval
#| eval: false
summary(cars)
```

**Both `false`, so nothing appears at all:**

```{r}
#| label: echo-eval-neither
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
summary(cars)
```

## `message` and `warning` {#sec-message-warning}

**Both a message and a warning are shown (the default):**

```{r}
#| label: message-warning-both
message("This is a message.")
warning("This is a warning.")
mean(c(1, 2, 3))
```

**`message: false` hides the message but keeps the warning:**

```{r}
#| label: message-warning-no-message
#| message: false
message("This is a message.")
warning("This is a warning.")
mean(c(1, 2, 3))
```

**Both suppressed, leaving only the result:**

```{r}
#| label: message-warning-neither
#| message: false
#| warning: false
message("This is a message.")
warning("This is a warning.")
mean(c(1, 2, 3))
```

## `output` {#sec-output}

`output: false` hides the result, but the code still runs.

```{r}
#| label: output-demo
#| output: false
a <- runif(100)
mean(a)
```

The chunk above printed nothing. The chunk below proves it ran anyway, because
the object `a` exists:

```{r}
#| label: output-demo-check
length(a)
```

## `include` {#sec-include}

`include: false` hides the code *and* the result. It is what you put on a setup
chunk that loads packages.

```{r}
#| label: include-demo
#| include: false
b <- runif(100)
```

Nothing from that chunk appears above, yet `b` was created:

```{r}
#| label: include-demo-check
length(b)
```

## Figure options {#sec-figure-options}

This chunk sets the size, the alignment, and the caption of the figure it
produces.

```{r}
#| label: fig-options
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: "Pressure rises sharply with temperature."
plot(pressure)
```

Change `fig-align` to `left` or `right`, or change `fig-width`, and render again
to see the effect.

## `code-fold` {#sec-code-fold}

`code-fold: true` collapses the code behind a button the reader can open,
instead of removing it from the document.

```{r}
#| label: code-fold-demo
#| code-fold: true
hist(yield, main = "Distribution of yield")
```

## `error` {#sec-error}

By default a failing chunk stops the whole render. `error: true` lets the
document build anyway and prints the error where it happened.

```{r}
#| label: error-demo
#| error: true
log("a")
```

# Reading a data file {#sec-reading-files}

By default R looks for a file in the folder holding this qmd file:

```{r}
#| label: read-relative
#| eval: false
corn <- read.csv("corn_price.csv")
```

Inside an R Project, `here()` builds the path from the project root instead, so
the same line works from any folder and on any computer:

```{r}
#| label: read-here
#| eval: false
corn <- read.csv(here::here("data", "corn_price.csv"))
```

Both chunks use `eval: false`, so they are shown but not run. Remove that option
once you have a file of your own to read.

# Caching {#sec-caching}

```{r}
#| label: cache_1
#| cache: true
#| eval: false

#--- repeat steps 1-3 B times ---#
MC_sim <- function(i) {
  N <- 50000 # sample size

  #--- steps 1 and 2 ---#
  mu <- rnorm(N) # the common term shared by both x and u
  x <- rnorm(N) + mu # independent variable
  v <- rnorm(N) + mu # error
  y <- 1 + x + v # dependent variable
  data <- data.frame(y = y, x = x)

  #--- OLS ---#
  reg <- lm(y ~ x, data = data) # OLS

  #--- return the coefficient on x ---#
  return(reg$coef["x"])
}

MC_results <- lapply(1:1000, MC_sim) |>
  unlist() |>
  mean()

MC_results
```

```{r}
#| label: cache_2
#| cache: true
#| eval: false
MC_results
```
